units.title: Terms and Simple Apprehension
units.blurb: The first act of the mind: grasping what a thing is. Terms, extension and comprehension, genus and species, the predicables, and logical division.

units.title: Categorical Propositions
units.blurb: The second act of the mind: judgment. The four standard forms A, E, I and O, translation into standard form, distribution, Venn diagrams and existential import.

units.title: The Square of Opposition
units.blurb: How the four forms about the same subject and predicate constrain one another: contradictories, contraries, subcontraries and subalterns.

units.title: Immediate Inference
units.blurb: New propositions from a single one: complements, conversion, obversion and contraposition, and chains of them.

units.title: Categorical Syllogisms
units.blurb: The third act of the mind: reasoning. Terms, mood and figure, testing by Venn diagrams and by the rules, and the valid forms.

units.title: Syllogisms in Everyday Form
units.blurb: Real arguments rarely arrive in standard form: reducing the number of terms, translating, filling in enthymemes, and chains called sorites.

units.title: Hypothetical and Disjunctive Syllogisms
units.blurb: Reasoning with if, or and not both: modus ponens and tollens, their fallacies, pure hypothetical, disjunctive and conjunctive syllogisms, and dilemmas.

topics.title: The Three Acts of the Mind
topics.short: Simple apprehension grasps a term, judgment joins terms into a proposition, and reasoning moves from propositions to a conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners treat a long phrase as a proposition. "The tall oak beside the river" is still one term; nothing is affirmed or denied until a verb joins it to a predicate.

topics.title: Terms
topics.short: A term is a word or phrase that names a class or an individual; singular terms name one thing, general terms name a class.
topics.trouble: Learners count words instead of ideas. "Large brown dogs" is one general term, and "the first president of the United States" is one singular term.

topics.title: Extension and Comprehension
topics.short: A term's extension is the set of things it applies to; its comprehension (intension) is the set of features it implies.
topics.trouble: Learners expect both to grow together. As comprehension grows (dog, then black dog, then small black dog), extension shrinks or stays the same.

topics.title: Genus and Species
topics.short: A genus is a wider class divided into species; the same class can be a species of one genus and a genus of narrower species.
topics.trouble: Learners use the biology ranks. In logic, genus and species are relative: "polygon" is a species of "shape" and a genus of "triangle".

topics.title: The Predicables
topics.short: A predicate can relate to its subject as genus, species, difference, property (always goes with it) or accident (may or may not).
topics.trouble: Property and accident are easy to confuse. A property follows from what the thing is (every triangle has angles summing to 180°); an accident does not (this triangle is red).

topics.title: Logical Division
topics.short: A good division splits a genus into species by one principle, so that the parts are exclusive and together exhaustive.
topics.trouble: Learners mix principles ("books: novels, hardcovers, library books"), so the parts overlap and some books fit nowhere or in two places.

topics.title: Categorical Propositions
topics.short: A categorical proposition relates two classes: quantifier, subject term, copula (are or are not) and predicate term.
topics.trouble: Learners take the grammatical subject or verb for the logical terms. In "All whales are mammals that breathe air", the predicate term is "mammals that breathe air".

topics.title: The Four Forms: A, E, I, O
topics.short: A: All S are P. E: No S are P. I: Some S are P. O: Some S are not P. Quantity is universal or particular; quality is affirmative or negative.
topics.trouble: Reading "some" as "some but not all": in logic, "Some S are P" means at least one, and it stays true even if all S are P.

topics.title: Putting Statements in Standard Form
topics.short: Turn verbs into "are" plus a class, singular statements into "All S are P", and words like "every", "none" and "a few" into the four quantifiers.
topics.trouble: Learners write "All S are not P" for "No S are P". "All that glitters is not gold" means "Some things that glitter are not gold", an O proposition.

topics.title: Only, None But and All Except
topics.short: "Only S are P" and "None but S are P" become "All P are S"; "All except S are P" makes two claims.
topics.trouble: Learners keep the order: "Only members may vote" does not say all members vote; it says all voters are members.

topics.title: Distribution of Terms
topics.short: A term is distributed when the proposition says something about every member of its class: A distributes S, E both, I neither, O the predicate.
topics.trouble: Learners memorize the chart without the reason. "Some S are not P" excludes the S from all of P, so it speaks about every P.

topics.title: Venn Diagrams for Propositions
topics.short: Shade a region to show it is empty; put an X in a region to show something is there. A and E shade; I and O place an X.
topics.trouble: Learners shade the region a statement talks about instead of the region it says is empty. For "All S are P", shade the part of S outside P.

topics.title: Existential Import
topics.short: In the modern (Boolean) reading, A and E say nothing about whether S exists; I and O do. The traditional reading assumes the subject class is not empty.
topics.trouble: Learners assume "All unicorns are white" claims there are unicorns. On the Boolean reading it only says there are no non-white unicorns.

topics.title: The Square of Opposition
topics.short: A, E, I and O with the same terms sit at the corners of a square; its sides and diagonals name how their truth values are tied.
topics.trouble: Learners place the corners in the wrong spots. Universals on top (A left, E right), particulars below (I under A, O under E).

topics.title: Contradictories
topics.short: A and O, and E and I, are contradictories: exactly one of each pair is true.
topics.trouble: Learners give "No S are P" as the contradictory of "All S are P". It is the contrary; to deny "all" you need only "some are not".

topics.title: Contraries and Subcontraries
topics.short: A and E cannot both be true but can both be false; I and O cannot both be false but can both be true.
topics.trouble: Learners treat contraries as contradictories and conclude from "A is false" that E is true. Both can be false when some S are P and some are not.

topics.title: Subalternation
topics.short: On the traditional square, truth flows down from A to I and from E to O, and falsity flows up from I to A and from O to E.
topics.trouble: Learners send truth up the square: "Some S are P" being true does not make "All S are P" true.

topics.title: Inferences on the Square
topics.short: Given the truth value of one corner, work out each other corner as true, false or undetermined.
topics.trouble: Learners force a value when the right answer is "undetermined", especially for the corners linked only by subalternation or subcontrariety.

topics.title: The Modern Square
topics.short: Without existential import only the contradictory diagonals survive; contrariety, subcontrariety and subalternation can fail when a class is empty.
topics.trouble: Learners keep using subalternation in the Boolean reading: from "All dragons breathe fire" it does not follow that some dragon breathes fire.

topics.title: Term Complements
topics.short: The complement of a class is everything outside it: non-P. The complement of non-P is P.
topics.trouble: Learners use the opposite word instead of the complement: the complement of "winners" is "non-winners", not "losers", since some may not have played.

topics.title: Conversion
topics.short: Conversion swaps subject and predicate. It is valid for E and I, not for A or O (A converts only by limitation, on the traditional reading).
topics.trouble: Converting an A proposition: "All cats are animals" does not give "All animals are cats". This illicit conversion is one of the most common mistakes in reasoning.

topics.title: Obversion
topics.short: Obversion changes the quality (affirmative to negative or back) and replaces the predicate with its complement; it is valid for all four forms.
topics.trouble: Learners change the quality but forget to complement the predicate, or complement the subject instead.

topics.title: Contraposition
topics.short: Contraposition swaps subject and predicate and replaces both with their complements. It is valid for A and O, not for E or I.
topics.trouble: Learners use contraposition on E or I, or swap the terms without complementing them, which is just conversion.

topics.title: Chains of Immediate Inference
topics.short: Combine conversion, obversion, contraposition and the square to decide whether one proposition follows from another.
topics.trouble: Learners lose track of which steps are valid for which form, or slip in an invalid conversion partway through the chain.

topics.title: The Parts of a Syllogism
topics.short: A categorical syllogism has three propositions and three terms: the major term (predicate of the conclusion), minor term (subject of the conclusion) and middle term.
topics.trouble: Learners name the major term by size or by which premise comes first. The conclusion decides: its predicate is the major term, its subject the minor term.

topics.title: Standard-Form Syllogisms
topics.short: In standard form the major premise (with the major term) comes first, then the minor premise, then the conclusion.
topics.trouble: Learners keep the order in which the premises were spoken. Find the conclusion first, then put the premise with its predicate on top.

topics.title: Mood
topics.short: The mood is the three letters of the major premise, minor premise and conclusion, in that order, such as AII or EAE.
topics.trouble: Learners read the letters in the order the sentences appear rather than in standard-form order.

topics.title: Figure
topics.short: The figure (1 to 4) records where the middle term sits: subject then predicate, predicate twice, subject twice, or predicate then subject.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up figures 1 and 4. In figure 1 the middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor.

topics.title: Testing Syllogisms with Venn Diagrams
topics.short: Draw three circles, diagram both premises, and the syllogism is valid when the conclusion is already shown without drawing anything more.
topics.trouble: Learners diagram the conclusion too, then say the picture "matches". Only the premises are drawn; then you read the conclusion off the picture.

topics.title: Venn Tests with Particular Premises
topics.short: Diagram universal premises first; place an X in a region only if the other region it could go in is shaded, otherwise put it on the line.
topics.trouble: Learners drop the X into one region when the premise allows two, which can make an invalid syllogism look valid.

topics.title: Rules of the Syllogism: Distribution
topics.short: The middle term must be distributed at least once, and a term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise.
topics.trouble: Undistributed middle: "All dogs are animals; all cats are animals; so all cats are dogs." Both premises talk about only part of the animals.

topics.title: Rules of the Syllogism: Quality
topics.short: Two negative premises prove nothing; a negative premise requires a negative conclusion, and a negative conclusion requires a negative premise.
topics.trouble: Learners think two negative premises can still link the terms. If neither premise says what the middle term includes, the terms never meet.

topics.title: Naming a Syllogism's Fallacy
topics.short: Each broken rule has a name: undistributed middle, illicit major, illicit minor, exclusive premises, affirmative from a negative, the existential fallacy, four terms.
topics.trouble: Learners stop at the first broken rule they see. Check every rule; one syllogism can break several, and the names point to the exact flaw.

topics.title: The Valid Forms and Their Names
topics.short: Fifteen mood-and-figure combinations are valid on the modern reading, such as AAA-1 (Barbara), EAE-1 (Celarent) and AII-3 (Datisi).
topics.trouble: Learners learn the names without the forms. The vowels of each name give its mood: Barbara is AAA, Celarent is EAE, Ferio is EIO.

topics.title: Conditionally Valid Forms
topics.short: Nine more forms, such as AAI-1 and EAO-2, are valid only if a class is assumed to have members; the Venn test shows which class.
topics.trouble: Learners count AAI-1 as valid on the modern reading. It needs the assumption that the minor term's class is not empty, or it commits the existential fallacy.

topics.title: Reducing the Number of Terms
topics.short: When an argument seems to have four or more terms, use synonyms, complements and obversion to bring it down to three.
topics.trouble: Learners call the argument invalid for four terms when two of them are synonyms or complements, or treat terms as the same when the meaning has shifted.

topics.title: Syllogisms in Everyday Language
topics.short: Put each statement in standard form, find the three terms, arrange the syllogism, then test it by the rules or a Venn diagram.
topics.trouble: Learners test the argument before translating, or translate "only" the wrong way, which flips a valid argument into an invalid one.

topics.title: Enthymemes
topics.short: An enthymeme is a syllogism with a premise or the conclusion left unstated; supply the missing part so the syllogism is valid, then judge whether it is true.
topics.trouble: Learners supply a premise that makes the syllogism invalid, or one so strong that it is plainly false when a weaker true one would work.

topics.title: Sorites
topics.short: A sorites is a chain of premises that leads to one conclusion through several hidden intermediate conclusions; it is valid when every link is a valid syllogism.
topics.trouble: Learners check only the first and last premises. Each step in the chain must be a valid syllogism on its own.

topics.title: Hypothetical Propositions
topics.short: A hypothetical proposition joins an antecedent and a consequent: "If P, then Q". "Q if P", "P only if Q" and "Q provided that P" say the same.
topics.trouble: "Only if" reversed: "P only if Q" means "if P then Q", not "if Q then P". "You may drive only if you have a license" does not promise that a license lets you drive.

topics.title: Affirming the Antecedent (Modus Ponens)
topics.short: From "If P, then Q" and "P", conclude "Q".
topics.trouble: Learners reject a modus ponens because they doubt the first premise. Doubting a premise is a question about soundness; the form itself is valid.

topics.title: Denying the Consequent (Modus Tollens)
topics.short: From "If P, then Q" and "not Q", conclude "not P".
topics.trouble: Learners find modus tollens harder than modus ponens and wrongly reject it. If P would bring Q, and there is no Q, there was no P.

topics.title: The Two Conditional Fallacies
topics.short: Affirming the consequent (Q, so P) and denying the antecedent (not P, so not Q) are invalid; the consequent can come about some other way.
topics.trouble: Affirming the consequent is the most common formal fallacy. Show it with a counterexample where Q is true for a different reason.

topics.title: Pure Hypothetical Syllogism
topics.short: From "If P, then Q" and "If Q, then R", conclude "If P, then R"; the links must run in the same direction.
topics.trouble: Learners chain conditionals that do not share a middle in the right place, such as "If P then Q" and "If R then Q".

topics.title: Disjunctive Syllogism
topics.short: From "P or Q" and "not P", conclude "Q". From "P or Q" and "P", nothing follows about Q unless the "or" is exclusive.
topics.trouble: Affirming a disjunct: learners read every "or" as "one or the other but not both". Logic's "or" is inclusive unless the speaker rules out both.

topics.title: Conjunctive Syllogism
topics.short: From "Not both P and Q" and "P", conclude "not Q". From "not P", nothing follows.
topics.trouble: Learners deny one conjunct and conclude the other is true. "Not both" allows neither to be true.

topics.title: Dilemmas
topics.short: A constructive dilemma reasons from "If P then Q, and if R then S" and "P or R" to "Q or S"; a destructive dilemma from "not Q or not S" to "not P or not R".
topics.trouble: Learners mix the two patterns, affirming consequents in a destructive dilemma or denying antecedents in a constructive one, which makes it invalid.

topics.title: Answering a Dilemma
topics.short: Escape between the horns (show a third option), grasp a horn (deny a conditional premise), or offer a counterdilemma.
topics.trouble: Learners answer a valid dilemma by calling it invalid. A valid dilemma can only be answered by showing one of its premises is false.
